exam: A 25‑year‑old male with a mid‑shaft femur fracture arrives after a road‑traffic crash – what is your immediate management and why? — Assess ABCs, apply traction, give analgesia, obtain AP/lateral X‑ray; stabilise to prevent fat embolism.

You find a swollen lower leg with pain on passive stretch after a tibial fracture – what complication are you concerned about and what is the next step? — Compartment syndrome; remove dressings and arrange emergency fasciotomy.

An open tibial fracture is classified as Gustilo‑Anderson grade II – which antibiotics do you start and for how long? — Ceftriaxone (or cefazolin) plus metronidazole; continue for 48‑72 h until wound closure.

A patient with a distal radius fracture has a palpable radial pulse but decreased sensation in the median nerve distribution – what does this indicate? — Possible median nerve injury; urgent reduction and neurovascular reassessment.

In a district hospital without fluoroscopy, how would you manage a displaced supracondylar humerus fracture in a child? — Closed reduction under sedation, apply a posterior splint, and refer for pinning if reduction unstable.
Why is a well‑padded splint preferred over a rigid cast for the first 24 hours in a swollen ankle fracture? — To accommodate swelling and prevent compartment syndrome.

What are the key differences between external fixation and internal fixation for open fractures? — External fixation avoids implanting hardware into contaminated tissue, is quicker, and can be adjusted; internal fixation provides definitive stability but requires clean soft‑tissue envelope.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with a femoral fracture – what additional considerations are needed? — Prevent vaso‑occlusive crisis with adequate hydration, pain control, and avoid hypoxia; monitor for infection.
ai.title: Traumatic Fracture Management
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Approach to acute fractures in low‑resource settings, covering assessment, imaging, stabilization, definitive fixation and complications. Emphasises clinical decision‑making when diagnostics are limited.

b: Identify open vs closed fracture
Assess limb perfusion, sensation and movement
Prioritise life‑threatening injuries first
sections.p: Traumatic fractures are broken bones caused by high‑energy injury or low‑energy falls in osteoporotic bone. Prompt assessment prevents neurovascular loss, infection and long‑term disability.

b: Open fracture: Gustilo‑Anderson grades I‑III
Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch
Neurovascular injury: absent pulses, loss of sensation or motor function
sections.p: Classification (open/closed, intra‑ vs extra‑articular, proximal/distal), stability, and soft‑tissue condition guide treatment. In low‑resource hospitals, the AO/OTA system may be simplified to ‘stable vs unstable’.

b: Use a well‑padded splint for temporary immobilisation
Apply a traction device for femur or tibial shaft fractures when surgery is delayed
Refer open grade III or unstable intra‑articular fractures to a higher centre
sections.p: Most patients present to district hospitals with limited imaging. Clinical skills and basic radiography are essential to decide between splinting, traction, external fixation or referral for internal fixation.

t.b: Confirms fracture pattern, displacement and joint involvement; guides fixation choice
Detects cortical discontinuity and large hematoma; useful for distal limb fractures
Identifies arterial injury or nerve palsy; if abnormal, urgent reduction or vascular surgery is needed
Baseline for infection risk; rising values after fixation suggest osteomyelitis

b: Closed reduction and casting for simple, stable fractures
External fixation for open grade I‑II or severely comminuted fractures when internal fixation is not possible
Intramedullary nailing or plating at referral centre for unstable long‑bone fractures
Broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for open fractures; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function unknown
Analgesia with paracetamol and NSAIDs; avoid NSAIDs in patients with renal disease or active bleeding
sections.p: Treat the fracture, protect neurovascular structures, prevent infection and manage pain. Choose interventions that are feasible with available resources.

b: Missing compartment syndrome – leads to permanent muscle loss
Leaving an open fracture untreated – high risk of osteomyelitis
Applying a cast over a swollen limb – can cause ischemia
Using internal fixation without adequate soft‑tissue coverage – predisposes to infection
sections.p: Errors often stem from inadequate assessment, delayed reduction, or inappropriate fixation.

sections.p: Examiners test your ability to prioritise, recognise complications and adapt to limited resources.

whenToSeekHelp: Absent distal pulses or worsening pain despite splint – possible vascular injury
Progressive swelling, pain on passive stretch, or paresthesia – compartment syndrome
Fever, increasing wound discharge – early osteomyelitis
